title: The GIA turns a light on fluorescence
dek: From the fourth quarter the laboratory will add language to its reports separating fluorescence that changes a diamond's look from fluorescence that does not, addressing a stigma that has discounted a quarter to a third of all stones since the 1990s.
body: One of the most persistent discounts in diamonds is about to get a footnote. From the fourth quarter of 2026, the GIA will add clarifying language to its grading reports to distinguish when fluorescence changes a diamond's appearance from when it does not. The trade has called it one of the biggest steps a laboratory has taken to address a trait that between 25% and 35% of diamonds carry to some degree.

Fluorescence, the soft glow some diamonds give under ultraviolet light, has been priced as a defect for decades even though it rarely is one. In most stones it does nothing visible; in a small share it can lend a milky or oily cast to high-color goods, and the market long ago collapsed those two very different cases into a single penalty. Rapaport has published fluorescence discount estimates since 1993, tracking a haircut that persisted through every swing of the market.

The fix is information, not chemistry. By stating on the report whether the fluorescence actually affects the look of the specific stone, the GIA lets a buyer separate the harmless from the compromised, and lets a seller defend a price rather than accept a reflex discount. For a sizable, long-misunderstood slice of the market, transparency about the trait could carry real weight with the trade and the shopper alike.

The commercial stakes sit with the middle of the counter. Faint and medium fluorescence in the near-colorless grades is exactly the material a value-minded consumer buys, and a clearer report gives the honest retailer a tool to reclaim margin that the blanket stigma has been quietly bleeding away.

The desk's view: this is a rare case of a grading change that helps the buyer and the seller at once, by pricing a stone for what it looks like instead of what it might do. Read the new line when it lands, because a diamond that glows and shows nothing for it may be the best-value stone in the case.

title: Up nine percent, and the average ticket did the lifting
dek: US jewelry revenue rose 8.6% in the first half and 13% in June, but the average purchase price climbed about 19 to 20 percent. Fewer buyers, spending more: bracelets, pearls and higher-priced pieces carried the gain.
body: American jewelry sales grew through the first half of 2026, but the growth was priced, not counted. Retail revenue rose 8.6% over the six months and 13% year on year in June, according to point-of-sale figures compiled by Tenoris, while the average purchase price climbed roughly 19% for the half and 20% in June. The store is ringing up bigger tickets from a thinner crowd, a pattern that flatters the top line and hides a narrowing base.

The gain concentrated at the higher-priced end. Bracelets, tennis styles in particular, led with a 14% revenue increase and double-digit growth in what shoppers were willing to spend on them. Pearl jewelry had what analysts called a surprisingly strong first half. Pendants and earrings held their own but trailed the leaders. The through-line is that the pieces carrying the market are the ones with a higher entry price, not the impulse buys near the register.

The two diamond categories tell different stories. Natural-diamond jewelry grew revenue at a single-digit rate, with unit sales down but higher average selling prices making up the difference and gross margins holding firm. Lab-grown moved the opposite way: revenue rose almost entirely on more units sold, while the average amount spent stayed essentially flat. One engine runs on price discipline, the other on volume, and rising rough costs could yet press on the cheaper of the two.

Set against the wider economy, jewelry outran the mall. US retail sales overall rose just 0.2% in June as tax-refund tailwinds faded and shoppers turned cautious. Against that backdrop a double-digit jewelry month looks strong, but the composition matters: a market that grows by selling dearer goods to fewer hands rewards the specialist counter and squeezes the value end, where a shopper who used to trade up now often trades out.

The desk's view: nine percent is a headline a jeweler can live with, but the honest number underneath it is the one on the tag, not the till. Sell the bracelet and the strand of pearls while the appetite for a real purchase is there, because a market held up by price is only ever one nervous quarter from finding out how many buyers it actually has.

title: Chow Tai Fook up fifteen, and gold by the gram did it
dek: Chow Tai Fook's quarterly retail sales rose 15.1%, with Hong Kong and Macau up 44.8% and weight-based gold jewelry up 64% there as softer gold revived demand. Luk Fook gained 32%, Chow Sang Sang 16%.
body: Chow Tai Fook, Greater China's largest jewelry chain, reported retail sales value up 15.1% year on year for the quarter to June, its fiscal first quarter. Mainland China supplied 83.6% of the total and grew 10.7%; Hong Kong, Macau and other markets, a sixth of the business, jumped 44.8%. On a same-store basis the mainland's self-operated shops rose 19.6% and franchises 15.7%, while Hong Kong and Macau together climbed 41.7%, Hong Kong up 35% and Macau up 64.6%.

One product line did the work. Weight-based gold jewelry, sold by the gram rather than by design, saw same-store sales leap 38% in the mainland and 63.7% in Hong Kong and Macau, as a softer gold price after June's pullback pulled buyers back to the counter. Fixed-price, design-led jewelry told the opposite story, slipping about 1% in the mainland. When gold reads as value, shoppers buy the metal and skip the markup.

The pattern is regional, not a single company's. Luk Fook posted quarterly retail sales up 32% and Chow Sang Sang up 16% over the same window, according to Rapaport's trade wire. Across the big Hong Kong-listed names, the story is the same: gold-as-savings is doing the selling, and the strength runs deepest where local buyers treat a chain necklace as a store of wealth rather than an accessory.

Yet the footprint is shrinking even as sales rise. Chow Tai Fook closed a net 258 mainland locations in the quarter, ending June with 5,434 points of sale, part of a multi-year rationalization of a once-sprawling network. Its April-launched Dawn Collection cleared more than HK$870 million, and the group leaned on brand upgrades to lift average prices. Investors stayed cool: the shares traded down about 2% and are off roughly 13% over six months.

The desk's view: a 64% surge in gold jewelry is a metal story wearing a retail costume, and metal stories turn. The chains booking these numbers are selling grams while gold sits just off a record; the test is whether the same shoppers come back for a diamond or a design once the bullion trade cools, or whether the counter has simply become a savings account with a clasp.

title: Silver up two percent, and the gold ratio tightens to 69
dek: Silver added about 2% on Friday to roughly $58 while gold held near $4,061, compressing the gold-silver ratio to about 69.5 from 70.7 at midweek. Both metals mark time before the Fed's July 29 decision.
body: Silver did the moving as the week closed. The white metal rose about 2% on Friday to roughly $58 an ounce while gold sat little changed near $4,061, tightening the gold-silver ratio to about 69.5 from 70.7 at midweek. It is a small compression, but a telling one: when both metals stall, the one that keeps a bid is usually the one carrying an industrial story as well as a monetary one.

Everything now waits on Washington. The Federal Reserve meets July 28 and 29, and a hold is widely expected; futures put the odds of a hike next week near a third and closer to four-in-five by September. Gold has largely priced the pause, which is why the tape has gone quiet. The move, when it comes, will be about tone rather than the decision itself, and a hawkish surprise would give the metal a reason to slip toward $4,000.

The cross-currents are unusually loud for a quiet tape. Crude has pushed to six-week highs on renewed US strikes on Iran and Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, lifting inflation expectations, and two-year Treasury yields have reached a seventeen-month high. Higher yields raise the cost of holding metal that pays no coupon, a headwind for gold, yet coin and bar premiums are holding firm as physical buyers treat anything under $4,100 as a level to accumulate rather than a top to sell.

Silver's edge in that standoff is its second job. Roughly half its demand is industrial, from solar cells to electronics, and that leg draws incremental buying when the rate path is uncertain and the monetary trade is stuck. A ratio near 69 is still historically wide, which is the bullish case the silver desk keeps making: if gold cannot break higher, the cheaper metal has the room to close the gap.

The desk's view: a compressing ratio in a parked market is the sound of money looking for the exit that still moves. For the counter it barely registers, because a chain sold by the gram tracks gold, not silver, but for anyone trading the metals into Wednesday the signal is the same one it has been all month, that the next real move is the Fed's to give.

title: Antwerp runs short of goods, and the buyers turn to India
dek: A summer shortage of polished goods in Antwerp is steering buyers toward India, where small-stone prices are recovering and the IIJS show opens August 6. A new 10% US duty hangs over the whole trade.
body: The diamond trade is thinning into its summer lull, but not evenly. Rapaport's trade wire reports Antwerp running short of goods, a shortage that is pushing buyers toward India even as the calendar empties out. US wholesale is described as steady despite the seasonal slowdown, and the hubs that normally cycle stock among themselves are instead watching demand drift east to the source.

Underneath the quiet is a recovery that has legs at the small end. The RapNet Diamond Index for 0.30-carat goods rose 0.79% on the week and 4.25% over the month, while one-carat commercial stones firmed and the benchmark one-carat category slipped a marginal 0.11% on the week. Small and commercial goods are leading the turn again, the same shape the market showed in the spring, and that is precisely the segment India cuts best.

India is reading the moment as an opening. The trade heads into IIJS Premiere in Mumbai, which opens August 6 and runs to the tenth, with unusual optimism for a summer show, and a goods shortage in Antwerp only sharpens the pull toward a country that polishes roughly nine in ten of the world's diamonds by piece. If the recovery is real, the August floor in Mumbai is where it gets confirmed or denied.

The complication arrived last week in Washington. A new 10% US Section 301 duty on Indian goods went live July 24, landing on the exact trade now flowing India's way, while diamonds polished in the European Union keep their exemption, a quiet incentive to route US-bound finishing back through Antwerp. So the trade walks into August holding two things at once, a genuine recovery in the goods India makes and a fresh tax on selling them to its largest customer.

The desk's view: a shortage in one hub and a tax on another is the market telling cutters to pick a lane before the show opens. India has the goods the recovery wants and the tariff it does not, and the winners in Mumbai will be the houses that already know which stones go to New York through Antwerp and which stay home for everyone else.

title: Diavik is closed, and Rio Tinto still pulled 33,000 carats from it
dek: Rio Tinto recovered 33,000 carats from Diavik's remaining ore in the second quarter, months after the Canadian mine closed. Output fell 97% from a year earlier; the company will sell its final diamonds through year-end.
body: A mine that stopped digging is still producing diamonds. Rio Tinto recovered 33,000 carats from Diavik's remaining ore in the second quarter, months after the flagship Canadian operation closed in March, working through residual and stockpiled material rather than mining anything new. It is a coda, not a comeback, but it is a reminder that a diamond mine does not go dark the day the last truck leaves the pit.

The scale of the wind-down is stark in the numbers. Second-quarter diamond output plunged 97% both from the prior quarter and year on year, and first-half production came to 1.1 million carats, down 51% from the same period in 2025. Those are the arithmetic of closure: once the ore body is exhausted, volume collapses to whatever the plant can still recover from what remains above ground.

Diavik was Rio Tinto's last diamond asset, and its closure completes a deliberate exit from the business. The major shut the famous pink-producing Argyle mine in Western Australia in 2020 and walked away from the Fort a la Corne project in Canada in 2023, choosing to concentrate on metals and minerals. Rio has said it will continue to manufacture and sell its final diamond production at least through the end of 2026.

The timing gives those last carats an odd tailwind. Certified Canadian goods carry a provenance premium, and they enter a market where a 50% US tariff now sits on Canadian goods and the natural-diamond scarcity argument is building on the back of mine closures worldwide. The final run from a marquee Canadian mine reaches buyers who are short of exactly that story, even as the tariff complicates the route to the largest market for it.

The desk's view: the interesting number is not the 33,000 carats but the zero that follows them. Diavik's close removes a reliable source of large, well-documented Canadian rough for good, and in a trade learning to sell scarcity, the mines that shut this decade will do more for prices than any marketing budget the industry could buy.

title: Anglo picks the Penny group for De Beers, and starts a year-end clock
dek: Anglo American has named the Gareth Penny-led consortium its leading bidder for De Beers and expects to finalize the sale by the end of 2026, even as a two-year production pause looms at the Venetia mine.
body: Anglo American has put a name and a deadline on its exit from diamonds. The mining group has selected the consortium led by former De Beers chief Gareth Penny as its leading bidder for the company, and expects to finalize the sale by the end of 2026, according to Rapaport's trade wire. It is the clearest signal yet that the separation Anglo set in motion last year will actually close, and close this year.

The house being sold is priced at a cyclical low. De Beers reported an estimated first-half loss, with second-quarter rough sales down 44% year on year to $665 million and the average realized price down 32% to $105 a carat, even as production rose 88% in the quarter to leave first-half output up 46%. More stones for far less money is the shape of a market where rough sells about a third below where it stood a year ago.

Supply is being trimmed to fit. De Beers is planning a two-year production pause at Venetia, its flagship South African mine, a decision that pulls future carats out of a market already carrying too many. For a buyer, that is both the risk and the logic of the deal: take control at the bottom, when the seller is cutting output because prices will not carry it.

The stakes run beyond one transaction. The Penny consortium would inherit a brand still synonymous with natural diamonds at the moment lab-grown stones have hollowed out the low end and fresh US tariffs cross the trade routes. A year-end close would end Anglo's long diamond era and hand the industry's most storied name to owners betting that scarcity, not marketing, is what turns the cycle back up.

The desk's view: buying De Beers in this market is a wager that the worst is in the price, and the two-year Venetia pause says the sellers half-believe it too. Whoever signs by December gets the name, the pipeline and the problem all at once, and the first quarter of ownership will tell everyone whether they bought a floor or a trapdoor.

De Beers rough production increases, but prices, demand remain under pressure — Mining Weekly

title: Gold takes the counter; pearls and gem-set keep a quieter lane
dek: As gold jewelry dominates counters worldwide, the color side splits: pearls had a surprisingly strong first half in the US, while fixed-price gem-set pieces slipped about 1% in mainland China.
body: While bullion writes the headlines and gold jewelry drives counters from Mumbai to Hong Kong, the color side of the trade is quietly sorting itself into winners and casualties. In the United States, pearl jewelry posted what analysts called a surprisingly strong first half, one of the standout categories in a market that grew 8.6% overall. Pearls, priced on nacre, luster and match rather than on metal weight, held their own in a year when weight was everything.

The other end of the color trade gave ground. In mainland China, Chow Tai Fook's fixed-price jewelry, the design-led, gem-set pieces that carry a maker's markup, slipped about 1% on a same-store basis in the quarter to June, even as the chain's weight-based gold jewelry leapt 38%. When a gold chain reads as savings, a gem-set pendant has to justify itself on feeling, not value, and this year feeling lost the argument at the Chinese counter.

The split is really one question asked twice. When gold is cheap enough to buy as a store of wealth, design and color compete on emotion alone, and the categories that win are the ones with their own scarcity to sell. Tennis bracelets, up 14% in the US, show that diamonds still move when the format is right; pearls show that a stone with no substitute keeps its lane. The losers are the middle pieces bought as gifts and priced as commodities.

That is the argument high summer usually settles. The season's high-jewellery launches lean hard on craft, heritage and rare stones precisely because those are the things a gram of gold cannot offer, and in a year of record metal the maisons selling rarity have the cleaner story. The color desk that thrives now is the one that stops competing with bullion on price and starts competing with it on the one thing gold does not have, which is a face.

The desk's view: pearls and fine color are not losing to gold so much as being asked to prove they are not gold, and the good ones can. Sell the strand and the signed piece on rarity and hand, not on carat weight, because the shopper who wants value already bought the chain, and the one standing at the color case is there for something the metal counter cannot sell them.

title: Ten and twelve-and-a-half: the tariff wall comes back
dek: A new Section 301 regime puts 10% duties on jewelry from India, Canada and Britain and 12.5% on China, Thailand, Turkey and the UAE, effective July 24. Diamonds polished in the EU keep their exemption.
body: The Trump administration reset its tariff machinery on July 24, imposing fresh duties on imported jewelry, diamonds, gemstones and precious metals from roughly sixty countries. The legal footing is new: with earlier levies struck down when the Supreme Court invalidated the administration's use of emergency economic powers, the White House reached instead for Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, framing the action as a response to countries said to under-enforce prohibitions on forced labor. The practical effect is a two-band wall across the trade's supply map.

The higher band, 12.5%, falls on China, Hong Kong, Israel, Thailand, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates, the cutting floors, manufacturing centers and trading hubs that move a large share of the world's finished goods. The 10% band covers a longer list that includes India, Canada, Mexico, Indonesia, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the United Kingdom. For a business that sources across a dozen borders before a stone reaches a display case, almost every common route now carries a number it did not carry a week ago.

The exemptions are where the detail lives. Diamonds and gemstones polished in the European Union keep the exemption they already held, an advantage that quietly rewards Antwerp and Idar-Oberstein against Surat and Bangkok. The EU and Taiwan face a net-of-most-favored-nation approach that tops combined rates up to a 10% floor; Japan, South Korea and Switzerland are handled the same way under a 12.5% cap. Goods already in transit on July 24 are spared, a narrow window that importers spent the week trying to widen.

The trade's compliance voices read the move as a beginning rather than an end. "The story is not over; people need to continue to pay attention," said Sara Yood of the Jewelers Vigilance Committee, noting that additional Section 301 inquiries into manufacturing capacity could add further duties later. The new bands also stack onto country-specific measures already in force, including the 50% rate on Canadian goods and the separate action against Brazil, so a single shipment can now carry more than one layer.

The desk's view: a 10% floor is survivable; the uncertainty around it is not. The EU carve-out is the tell, quietly steering polished volume toward Antwerp and away from Surat, and the promise of further inquiries means no importer can price a spring order with confidence. Expect the near-term response to be the oldest one in the book: pull inventory forward, sit on the goods in transit, and pass what cannot be absorbed to the counter.

title: Surat does the math on ten percent
dek: India polishes roughly nine in ten of the world's diamonds by volume, and the United States is its largest customer. A 10% duty on Indian polished, live July 24, lands on a trade already thinned by cheap rough and soft margins.
body: No country has more exposed to the new tariff schedule than India, which cuts and polishes somewhere around ninety percent of the world's diamonds by piece count and sends a large slice of that output to American buyers. The 10% duty that took effect on July 24 is not the highest rate on the board, but it lands on the single busiest lane in the polished trade, and it lands at a moment when the men who own the wheels in Surat have the least room to give.

That thin room is the second story inside the first. Rough is cheap, with De Beers' realised price down about a third year on year, but cheap rough has not rescued cutters, because polished prices have fallen alongside it and the spread that pays a factory's wages has stayed narrow. Surat spent the past year trimming shifts and idling benches; a fresh 10% at the border is a cost that has to be split three ways, among the exporter who books the sale, the American importer who takes the goods, and the shopper who eventually pays the ticket.

The exemption for European-polished stones sharpens the choice. A diamond that leaves India as rough, travels to Antwerp to be polished and enters the United States as EU goods can, on paper, sidestep the duty that the same stone would carry if finished in Gujarat. Re-routing at scale is neither quick nor free, and rules of origin will be argued over for months, but the incentive now points away from the world's largest cutting center, which is precisely the outcome its exporters feared.

India's trade bodies have spent the season lobbying against exactly this, arguing that duties on polished goods punish a labor-intensive industry that competes on cost. The near-term arithmetic is unforgiving: at a 10% rate on a category already running on single-digit margins, some orders simply do not clear, and the ones that do move slower. The question the trade will spend August answering is who, along that chain from bench to counter, is left holding the difference.

The desk's view: the tariff does not fall on India so much as on the seam between India and America, and seams are where trades tear. A 10% wall around the cheapest labor in the pipeline invites the goods to route around it, and the EU carve-out draws the map. For Surat, the danger is not this quarter's duty but the precedent that finishing a stone at home has become the expensive option.

title: Gold near $4,061 waits on the Fed
dek: Gold ended the week around $4,061 an ounce, up roughly 2% on the week but still short of $4,100, as traders positioned for a Federal Reserve widely expected to hold rates when it meets July 28 and 29.
body: Gold closed the week near $4,061 an ounce, a gain of about 0.3% on Friday and roughly 2% across the five sessions, but still on the wrong side of the $4,100 line it has been probing for a fortnight. The metal is holding a high plateau rather than breaking out, which is the posture of a market waiting for someone else to move first. This week, that someone is the Federal Reserve.

The policy committee meets July 28 and 29, and the consensus expects it to leave rates where they are, echoing the European Central Bank's hold on Thursday. The case for standing still got firmer late in the week when jobless claims came in at 187,000 against a forecast of 212,000, a labor market stronger than the models penciled in. A stronger jobs picture cuts both ways for gold: it eases recession fear, but it keeps alive the prospect of higher rates later in the year if inflation stays above target.

That rate-and-gold relationship is the whole game at these levels. Higher interest rates raise the opportunity cost of holding an asset that pays no coupon, so a hawkish surprise on Wednesday would give the metal a reason to slip back toward $4,000, while any dovish tilt would hand it the excuse to test $4,100 again. The white metals told their own story on Friday: silver added about 1.2% to $58.22, while platinum slipped 1.1% to $1,574.

For the jewelry trade, the number that matters is less the daily print than the shelf it sits on. Gold has spent July defending $4,000 rather than charging past it, and a market that merely holds a record is easier to design around than one that lurches. Manufacturers pricing autumn collections are treating $4,000 as the floor and $4,100 as the ceiling until the Fed says otherwise.

The desk's view: this is a coiled-spring week, and the spring is wound by Wednesday's statement, not by the tape itself. Gold at $4,061 is neither cheap nor frightened; it is parked. The risk is asymmetric for the counter, because another leg higher squeezes margins that record metal has already stretched thin, while a pullback toward $4,000 would be the first good news the gold bench has had in a month.

title: Platinum runs short a fourth year, and still slips
dek: The World Platinum Investment Council sees a 297,000-ounce supply deficit in 2026, a fourth straight shortfall, even as spot platinum fell about 1% Friday to $1,574 and jewelry demand for the metal drops 12%.
body: Platinum is that rare thing in commodities, a metal the world keeps running short of while its price refuses to celebrate. The World Platinum Investment Council now forecasts a 297,000-ounce deficit for 2026, the fourth consecutive year in which supply falls short of demand, and yet spot platinum slipped about 1% on Friday to $1,574 an ounce. Scarcity on paper and softness on the screen are, for now, coexisting.

The demand mix explains the tension. Total platinum demand is set to fall about 9% to 7,674,000 ounces, dragged by a 12% drop in jewelry use and a 2% dip in automotive, where the metal's traditional home in catalytic converters keeps shrinking. What holds the market in deficit is elsewhere: industrial demand climbs 9% to 2,238,000 ounces on new glass-making capacity, and bar-and-coin investment jumps 27% to 718,000 ounces as buyers treat platinum as the cheap cousin of gold.

Supply, meanwhile, is barely moving. Mine output is projected flat while recycling grows about 9%, lifting total supply only 2% and leaving the shortfall to be filled from above-ground stocks that the council expects to cover less than three months of global demand by the end of the year. "The market continues to be undersupplied, and platinum demand is well insulated," said the council's chief executive, Trevor Raymond, pressing the investment case that price alone has yet to make.

For the jewelry bench, the 12% fall in platinum demand is the line that stings, and it is a demand problem, not a supply one. High gold has not sent buyers to platinum in the numbers the metal's backers hoped; instead it has thinned the whole precious-jewelry category, and platinum, always the connoisseur's choice, feels it first. The deficit is real, but a deficit driven by collapsing jewelry offtake is a strange kind of bull case.

The desk's view: platinum's shortage is a supply story wearing a demand problem, and markets pay for the problem before they pay for the story. Four straight deficits should have lit a fire under the price; instead the metal sits at $1,574 because the buyers who would bid it up, jewelers and carmakers, are both stepping back. The investment thesis is sound and early, which on a trading desk is another word for wrong, until it isn't.

title: India buys the dip as gold falls ten percent
dek: Indian gold fell about 10% in June to a six-month low near 141,000 rupees per 10 grams, and buyers came back: listed jewellers logged 30-60% revenue growth, though old-gold trade-ins now fund up to 55% of counter sales.
body: When the gold price finally blinked, India bought. The World Gold Council's July read on the market records a roughly 10% fall in the domestic price during June, to about 141,000 rupees per 10 grams, its lowest in six months, tracking an 11% slide in the international price to near $4,000. Overall consumer demand stayed subdued, the council notes, but the drop was enough to pull jewelry buyers off the sidelines they had occupied through the spring's records.

The listed chains felt it first. Major organized jewellers reported revenue growth of 30% to 60% year on year for the April-to-June quarter, a number that looks heroic until the composition is examined. As much as 43% to 55% of jewelry sales were funded not by fresh money but by old gold traded back across the counter, with exchange volumes rising a further 10% to 20% after a duty change nudged households to recycle rather than import.

Investment demand told a divided story. Gold exchange-traded funds took in 34.4 billion rupees of net inflows in June, the most since February, lifting holdings 2.2 tonnes to 119 tonnes, and digital-gold transaction values rose to 25.5 billion rupees. Bars and coins, the traditional hoard, cooled at the same time, a sign that the newer, screen-based ways of owning gold are quietly taking share from the safe at home.

The import line shows how much the froth has come off. June gold imports fell 42% from May to $1.97 billion, with volume down to somewhere between 16 and 22 tonnes from 29 tonnes, and gold's share of the country's merchandise import bill dropped to 3% from 17% in January. The domestic market even swung to a discount averaging about $20 an ounce in early July, a world away from the $150 premium of May.

The desk's view: this is a recycling recovery, not a demand boom, and the two are easy to confuse on a quarterly slide. When more than half of what crosses the counter is yesterday's gold coming back, revenue can grow while fresh appetite stays flat, and imports can fall while shops look busy. India will buy every dip in gold; the open question is whether it will still buy the metal at a new high, or only the story of a bargain.

sources.title: India gold market update: Mixed demand signals — World Gold Council

title: List prices up, resale down: the watch gap narrows
dek: Swiss brands raised US retail prices about 7% for 2026 while the secondary market slid roughly 8% to two-year lows, squeezing the premium that once made a steel sports watch behave like an investment.
body: Two lines that used to move together are now moving apart. Swiss brands opened 2026 with US retail increases of about 7%, led by Rolex, Tudor and Audemars Piguet, while the secondary market spent the year sliding, with index trackers putting the broad decline near 8% and both Rolex and Patek Philippe touching two-year lows. The list price went up; the street price went down; the gap between them is the whole subject.

That gap is where the last cycle's speculation lived. At the 2022 peak, a steel sports Rolex or a Nautilus traded far above its boutique price, and the premium was the reason people queued for waitlists they never intended to wear. As the secondary market has cooled through 2026, that premium has compressed toward zero and, on many references, below it, which turns a flip into a loss and a waitlist into a formality rather than a lottery ticket.

The decline is not uniform, and the exceptions are instructive. Rolex's secondary prices have held comparatively steady, the blue-chip behaving like a blue-chip, while Patek Philippe's broader range has been the weaker performer even as its scarcest complications keep setting gains. The market, in other words, is sorting: the truly rare still appreciates, the merely desirable is repricing toward what a watch is actually worth to someone who wants to own it.

For retailers, the narrowing gap is a mixed blessing. A secondary market that no longer trades at a fat premium removes the grey-market temptation that pulled buyers away from authorized doors, but it also strips the resale-value story that justified the primary purchase. Selling a $15,000 sports watch is harder when last year's model can be had for less than list on a screen, and the January price increase only widens that spread.

The desk's view: the era of the watch as a liquid asset is closing, and the counter should be glad of it. When the flip stops paying, the buyer who remains is the one who wanted the object rather than the arbitrage, and that is a healthier customer to build a business on. The brands raising list prices into a falling secondary market are betting that desire outlives speculation. On the evidence of the rarest Pateks, they may be right.

title: Furmanovich cuts Art Deco from straw and beetle-wing
dek: The Brazilian marquetry house has translated 1920s geometry into straw inlay, Shibayama, abalone and iridescent beetle-wing, a couture-level collection arguing that craft, not carat weight, is the luxury on offer.
body: Silvia Furmanovich, the São Paulo designer who built a house on the humble craft of marquetry, has turned her wood-and-straw technique on the most geometric decade in decorative history. Her new Art Deco collection, drawn up around the centenary of the 1925 Paris Exposition that gave the style its name, reads the 1920s not through diamonds and platinum but through texture, arranging chevrons, mosaics and spirals in materials most fine jewelers never touch.

The material list is the statement. Straw marquetry, the enchapado de tamo that is the house signature, sits alongside Japanese Shibayama inlay, mother-of-pearl and abalone, iridescent beetle-wing, black palm wood, coral and mirrored surfaces. Egyptomania and Japonisme, the two exotic currents that fed original Deco, return here as surface and pattern rather than as motif, filtered through the hands of Brazilian and Asian artisans the studio has spent years training.

It is a deliberate argument about where value sits. In a season when the natural-diamond price is falling and the lab-grown stone has made carat weight cheap, a collection that asks to be judged on the difficulty of its making rather than the size of its stones is making a case for craft as the last defensible luxury. The pieces debuted at Couture in Las Vegas in the spring and have been circulating through the trade press since.

"Jewelry has always been a form of cultural exploration," Furmanovich has said, and the collection wears that thesis openly, treating a brooch as a small piece of cabinetry and a cuff as a field for inlay. The approach does not scale the way a diamond line does, which is precisely the point; each piece is closer to a commissioned object than a stocked SKU, and priced accordingly.

The desk's view: this is the counter-programming the high end needs right now. As stones lose their scarcity, the houses that will hold their margins are the ones selling something a factory cannot copy overnight, and a beetle-wing mosaic set by hand is about as hard to copy as jewelry gets. Furmanovich is betting that when the diamond stops being rare, the labor around it becomes the thing worth paying for.

title: De Beers digs 88% more, banks 44% less
dek: Second-quarter rough output jumped 88% to 7.8 million carats even as the average price fell 32% to $105 a carat. Revenue slid 44% to $665 million. Production is rising into the weakest market in a generation.
body: The headline number from De Beers' second-quarter production report, published July 23, looks like a recovery: 7.8 million carats out of the ground, up 88% on the same quarter a year ago, when the miner had throttled output to defend prices. First-half production reached 14.91 million carats, up 46%. Botswana did the heavy lifting, raising output 107% to 5.5 million carats; Venetia in South Africa added 700,000 carats, up 24%; Gahcho Kué in Canada contributed a million; only Namibia, at half a million carats, held flat. On the mine plan, this is a business running closer to capacity again.

The price line tells the opposite story. The average realised price fell 32% year on year to $105 a carat, and De Beers' rough price index, its measure of like-for-like pricing, was down 16%. Second-quarter sales reached 7.1 million carats, but revenue from them fell 44% to $665 million; first-half rough revenue was $1.31 billion, down 23%. Producing more into a market that pays less is the arithmetic of a company that has decided inventory on the balance sheet is worse than stones sold cheaply.

The guidance carries its own warning. De Beers held full-year production guidance at 21 to 26 million carats, a wide band that already builds in planned maintenance and, more tellingly, an expected pause at Venetia in the second half. The mine that just posted a 24% output gain is scheduled to go quiet, a reminder that the 88% rebound is measured against a deliberately starved 2025 rather than against health. Lab-grown competition, the company noted, continues to press the lower-value end of the book while premium goods hold firmer.

Around the production report sits the larger question of ownership. Anglo American, De Beers' parent, has flagged that underlying earnings at the diamond unit will be negative for the first half and has repeated that it is progressing the sale of the business while cutting costs. Reports last week named a consortium led by former De Beers chief executive Gareth Penny as the front-runner to buy the 85% stake, though Anglo has declined to confirm. A full-year 2025 earnings loss of $511 million is the backdrop against which any buyer is doing its sums.

The desk's view: a miner that digs 88% more and earns 44% less is not recovering; it is clearing its throat before a sale. The production rebound flatters a comparison against a year De Beers spent holding stones back, and the Venetia pause tells you management still does not trust the market to absorb the goods. For a buyer, the appeal is the brand and the reserves, not this quarter's tape. For the trade, the signal is simpler: rough is cheap and getting cheaper, and the company that sets the price has stopped pretending otherwise.

title: Gold defends $4,000 as oil clears $100
dek: Bullion held $4,028 on Friday, a whisker above the $4,000 line, as Brent crude topped $100 and the ten-year yield reached 4.70%. Traders now price an 80% chance of a September rate rise, up from 68%.
body: Gold spent Friday doing what it has done for most of July: defending a line. Spot bullion changed hands near $4,028 an ounce, a slender margin above the $4,000 level that has become the market's psychological floor, after sliding through the back half of the week from a two-week peak above $4,160. The metal is caught between two forces that rarely pull the same way, and this week they are pulling hard in opposite directions.

On one side is the safe-haven bid. Brent crude pushed above $100 a barrel as geopolitical risk, a widening conflict around Iran and strikes on shipping in the Gulf, fed straight into energy prices. Oil at three figures is an inflation input, and inflation is, in the long run, gold's friend. Central banks agree with the thesis: roughly 45% of those surveyed say they intend to add gold over the coming year, a structural bid that does not blink at a single week's tape.

On the other side is the cost of holding a metal that pays no coupon. The same oil-driven inflation scare has pushed the two-year Treasury toward a seventeen-month high and the ten-year to 4.70%, and it has moved the market's read on the Federal Reserve. Fed-funds futures now imply an 80% probability of a rate increase in September, up from 68% a week ago. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of gold, and that is the weight currently pinning it just above $4,000 rather than letting it run.

The white metals, quieter, carried the week's marks into Friday with little conviction: silver near $58.90 an ounce, platinum around $1,629 and palladium near $1,275, none of them moving enough to verify a fresh print. For a jeweller costing a collection, the number that matters is not the daily wiggle but the shape: gold has spent a month refusing to break either way, and a $4,000 handle has held through a war premium, a hot inflation scare and a hawkish Fed repricing.

The desk's view: a metal that will not fall on higher rates and will not rally on a war premium is a metal in equilibrium, and equilibrium at $4,000 is its own kind of statement. The September meeting is now the hinge; an 80% hike bet is close enough to consensus that a hold would jolt gold up and a hike is largely in the price. For the bench, plan around $4,000 as the floor it has earned, not the ceiling it once was.

title: The Apollo Gallery reopens, minus the crown jewels
dek: Nine months after thieves took over $100 million in French royal jewels in a seven-minute raid, the Louvre's Apollo Gallery reopened July 22. The jewels will not return to it. Four suspects are in custody; the stones are still gone.
body: The Louvre reopened its Apollo Gallery to the public on July 22, nine months after the October 2025 heist that turned the most famous jewel room in the world into a crime scene. Visitors filed back beneath the gilded ceiling to find the cases that once held the French crown jewels empty. The museum has decided the gallery will no longer display royal jewellery at all; the surviving pieces are being moved to a more secure location, and the Apollo reverts to its older function as a state gallery.

The raid it is recovering from was a study in speed. A crew disguised as construction workers parked a truck-mounted basket lift against the building's river façade, rode it to a first-floor window, cut through with an angle grinder and a disc cutter, lifted jewelled pieces valued at more than $100 million from their cases, and were back on motorcycles in roughly seven minutes. It was less a burglary than a logistics exercise, executed against a national museum in daylight.

The investigation has produced arrests but no jewels. Four suspects are in custody; by the account reported this week, they say they were hired hands and have declined to name whoever commissioned the theft. No stones have been recovered, and the working assumption across the trade is grim: pieces this recognisable are worth far more broken and recut than intact, which means the French crown jewels may already have ceased to exist as the objects the catalogue describes.

The reopening doubles as a policy moment. France's culture ministry has announced a national plan to harden security at museums and national collections, an admission that the vulnerability was systemic rather than local. The art-recovery specialist Christopher Marinello put the lesson bluntly: if thieves can get into the Louvre, they can get in anywhere. For a jewellery trade that leans on museums to display, authenticate and lend prestige to historic stones, that is an uncomfortable sentence to sit under.

The desk's view: the Louvre's real decision this week was not to reopen the room but to empty it, and that is the more honest response. A gallery that cannot protect the crown jewels should not hold them, and moving them to a vault concedes what nine months of investigation confirmed, that display and security had drifted too far apart. The wider bill lands on every institution that borrows historic jewels to draw a crowd; insurers and lenders will now price the Apollo raid into every loan agreement. Prestige, it turns out, has a security deposit.

title: Emeralds hold at $146 a carat; rubies wait their turn
dek: Gemfields' higher-quality emerald auction took $26.8 million, selling 36 of 37 lots at an average $146.08 a carat. A 10% slide in the rupee weighed on Indian buyers, and the miner is treading carefully on rubies after a $51 million loss.
body: Gemfields' latest auction of higher-quality rough emeralds closed at $26.8 million, a result the miner will take as a steadying hand under a jittery colour market. Held in London over 4 to 21 May and reported in recent days, the sale cleared 36 of its 37 lots, 97% by number and 99% by weight, at an average of $146.08 a carat. In a year when almost every hard-luxury category has been marked down, an emerald book that sells through at those prices reads as quiet strength.

The stones come from Kagem, the Zambian mine Gemfields owns 75%, with the Industrial Development Corporation of Zambia holding the rest. Adrian Banks, the company's managing director of product and sales, framed the demand as real but cautious: appetite for higher-quality emeralds remains stable, he said, while the market exercises a degree of caution against a backdrop of geopolitical tension and macro uncertainty. The caveat had a currency attached. The Indian rupee has lost roughly 10% against the dollar since September 2025, and India is where much of the world's rough colour is cut; a weaker rupee makes every dollar-priced lot dearer at the bench.

What Gemfields did not do this cycle is as telling as what it did. The company has been holding back on rubies, pacing its higher-value ruby offering rather than forcing goods into an uncertain room. That is a producer managing scarcity deliberately, the colour-market equivalent of De Beers keeping rough in the vault, except that Gemfields is doing it from a position of financial strain rather than strength.

The strain is real. Gemfields posted a $51 million loss for 2025, and it has spent this year raising capital and trimming to steady the balance sheet. An emerald sale that performs is oxygen, but a single strong auction does not reverse a loss of that size. The read across the colour trade is that the top of the market, signed, high-clarity, provenance-backed stones, is holding, while the broader book waits on the same macro clouds hanging over diamonds and watches.

The desk's view: $146 a carat with a 99%-by-weight clearance is a genuinely good number, and it says the ceiling of the colour market is intact even as the middle sags. But read the ruby decision and the rupee line together and the picture sharpens: this is a producer rationing supply to protect price because it cannot afford a weak print. Emeralds held the line this week. Whether rubies get the same disciplined treatment, or get pushed to market to plug a hole, is the number the desk will be watching next.

title: Small stones lead again as one-carat goods slip
dek: RapNet's June index rose 4.2% for 0.30-carat diamonds and 1.3% for half-carats, while the one-carat benchmark fell 0.7%. Inventory cuts, not fresh demand, are doing the lifting at the small end.
body: The recovery in polished diamonds, such as it is, keeps arriving from the bottom of the size chart. The RapNet Diamond Index for June, published mid-July, rose 4.2% for 0.30-carat stones and 1.3% for half-carats, each an acceleration on May's gains. The three-carat category edged up 0.4%, turning positive after a soft spring. The exception sat in the middle of the counter: the one-carat benchmark, the size most shoppers picture when they picture a diamond, slipped 0.7%.

The mechanism matters more than the percentages. Rapaport attributes the firmness in smalls to inventory reductions rather than a wave of new buying; dealers have stopped restocking melee and small goods, and the thinner shelves are letting prices correct upward. It is a supply story dressed as a demand story, the market clearing an overhang rather than discovering fresh appetite. Prices rise because there is less to sell, not because more people are buying.

The size split is its own signal about who is spending. Larger goods, two carats and up in the G-to-I colour, VS-to-SI clarity band, remained the strongest sellers in the United States, the province of buyers less troubled by the macro clouds. Rounds in the one-to-two-carat range showed what Rapaport called only mild improvement. The barbell that has defined the polished market all year is still there: the top holds, the entry firms on scarcity, and the mass-market middle where most engagement rings live stays soft.

Set against De Beers' rough report the same week, the polished tape completes a coherent picture. Rough is being produced in volume and sold cheap; polished is recovering only where supply has been deliberately choked. Neither half of the pipeline is being pulled higher by consumers reaching for diamonds. Both are being managed, by miners holding grades back and by dealers refusing to restock, into the appearance of stability.

The desk's view: a 4.2% monthly gain in half-point goods sounds like spring, but a recovery built on empty shelves is a fragile thing, and the 0.7% dip in one-carat stones is the tell. The size that anchors the bridal counter is still drifting, and that is the number that pays the trade's rent. Until the one-carat line turns on real demand rather than the small end turning on thin inventory, the desk reads this as stabilisation, not recovery, the diamond market holding its breath, not catching it.

title: Lab-grown now costs 73% less; naturals win the ring back
dek: A study of appraisal data finds lab-grown diamonds priced 73% below naturals, up from a 27% gap in 2019. As the discount widened, natural stones reclaimed 57% of engagement rings, the reversal grown diamonds were supposed to prevent.
body: The gap between a natural diamond and its laboratory twin has become a canyon. Analysing appraisal and insurance records from March 2019 through May 2025, the insurance-technology firm BriteCo found lab-grown diamonds now priced roughly 73% below comparable naturals. In 2019 the discount was 26.6%. By 2025 it had widened to 72.8%. A one-carat natural averages around $4,200 in the data; its grown equivalent sells for about $1,000 or less.

The widening is a supply story with a demand twist. Grown-diamond output from Chinese and Indian producers has climbed relentlessly, and a manufactured good made in ever-greater volume behaves the way manufactured goods do: the price falls toward the cost of making it. Natural prices, having spiked through the pandemic years, have drifted back down but nothing like as far. The two lines have been diverging for six years, and the distance between them is now the widest it has ever been.

Here is the twist the grown-diamond industry did not script. As lab-grown got cheaper, it did not consolidate its grip on the bridal market; it started to lose it. BriteCo's data has natural stones back to 57.3% of engagement rings sold in late 2024 and early 2025, a reversal from a lab-grown peak of 47.7% share. The cheaper the grown stone became, the more it read to some shoppers as a fashion purchase rather than an heirloom, and an engagement ring is the last place many buyers want to feel they economised.

For retailers the divergence is a margin puzzle with no clean answer. A grown-diamond sale is a smaller ticket that keeps shrinking as wholesale prices fall, which is why several chains have hedged by selling both and steering the emotional pitch toward natural. The risk is a two-tier counter that trains the customer to see the grown stone as the discount option and the natural as the real one, useful for natural margins, corrosive for the grown-diamond brand the same store spent five years building.

The desk's view: the lab-grown industry made a bet that price was the whole game, and winning on price turns out to have been the losing move. At a 73% discount the grown stone has priced itself into a different product category, beautiful, honest, and no longer competing for the meaning a buyer wants an engagement ring to carry. Naturals reclaiming the ring is not nostalgia; it is what happens when one side of a market keeps cutting price until the cut becomes the message. The number to watch is not the discount. It is the share.

title: Trophies carry Sotheby's to $31.4 million; a pink walks
dek: Sotheby's New York High Jewelry sale of 13 June 2025 made $31.4 million with 95% sold, led by a $3.2 million Graff diamond ring. Down the street, Phillips withdrew a 3.03-carat fancy pink when bids missed its reserve.
body: The trophy end of the jewellery market is still doing the work. Sotheby's High Jewelry sale in New York on 13 June 2025 made $31.4 million with 95% of lots finding buyers, a result led, as these sales almost always are, by a handful of exceptional single stones rather than broad depth. That night is a marker rather than a bulletin, and it is read here as one: the sale it belongs to is more than a year behind the tape this paper prints each morning, and the room described below is the room of that June, not of this one.

The board read like a tour of what money still chases. A Graff ring set with a 35-carat D-colour diamond took $3.2 million. A Marcus & Co. sautoir centred on a 9.6-carat Burmese ruby and a 2.02-carat fancy vivid blue diamond tied at $1.8 million apiece. A JAR ring holding an 8.62-carat Colombian emerald made $1.6 million, and a 1930s Kashmir sapphire ring of 7.5 carats reached $1.4 million. Colour, provenance and signature, the three things a factory cannot print, carried the night.

Sotheby's framed it as continuity. Quig Bruning, the house's head of jewellery in the Americas, said provenance, rarity and exceptional craftsmanship continue to ignite the passions of collectors, and called the sale a great continuation of what he described as a phenomenal year for jewellery. The house has reason for the confidence: at the level where a single stone clears seven figures, the buyer pool has barely noticed the macro weather that has chilled the retail counter.

The counter-example was a short walk away, on the same week's calendar. Phillips withdrew the top lot of its own New York jewels sale, a 3.03-carat fancy intense pink diamond estimated at $1.2 million to $1.6 million, after bids failed to meet the reserve. A withdrawn headline lot is the auction world's quiet way of saying the estimate and the room disagreed, and it is a useful corrective to any story that the top is invincible. Even at the summit, price discovery still bites when a house aims too high.

Correction, 18 August 2026: this article was published on 24 July 2026 and reported Sotheby's New York High Jewelry sale of "June 13" without a year, framing it as a current result in "a year of soft mid-market tapes." The sale it describes closed on 13 June 2025. The 2026 edition of the same sale ran on 16 June 2026 and made $43.4 million with 98% of 119 lots sold, led by an unmounted 10.02-carat fancy intense blue diamond at $8.7 million. The error came from reading a source page without checking its own publication date, the trap this paper's own bureau desk screens for daily. Every figure in this article was correct as published for the sale it actually describes: the $31.4 million total, the 95% sell-through, the $3.2 million Graff ring, the Marcus & Co. sautoir, the JAR emerald, the Kashmir sapphire and the withdrawn Phillips pink. Only the year was missing, and the present tense it was written in was wrong.

The desk's view: $31.4 million at 95% sold is a strong night, but read it with the withdrawn pink and the lesson is precision, not exuberance. The market for singular, provenance-backed stones is genuinely intact; the market for aggressively estimated ones is not. Collectors are still paying for rarity they can name, a Kashmir sapphire, a Burmese ruby, a signed JAR, and passing on anything that feels priced for a hotter year than this one. The trophies carry the room. They no longer forgive a reserve set in the mood of the year before.

title: Swiss watch exports jump 11.2%, but the profit doesn't follow
dek: June's 11.2% export rebound was the strongest reading in a year and sent Swatch shares higher. Yet the group's half-year profit was CHF 16 million on CHF 3.12 billion of sales, half a percent. The volume is back; the margin is not.
body: The Swiss watch industry got its best headline in a year last week: exports rose 11.2% in June, according to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, an unexpected rebound after months of soft numbers, and Swatch Group shares jumped on the read-through. After a year in which the standard question was how much worse it could get, a double-digit export gain landed like a change of season.

Look past the shipment figure, though, and the profit line refuses to celebrate. Swatch Group's first-half revenue was CHF 3.12 billion, up about 9% at constant currency, with the United States up 27% and China including Hong Kong and Macau up 9%. Net profit for the same six months was CHF 16 million, roughly half a percent of sales. A company can grow its top line smartly and still hand almost none of it to the bottom, and that is precisely what a mass-and-mid-market watchmaker does when it is discounting to move stock and carrying the cost of a bloated inventory.

The divergence maps onto a split that has defined the whole watch year: shipments and sell-through are not the same thing. Exports measure what leaves Switzerland for the wholesale channel; they can rise on restocking and a soft base without a single extra watch reaching a wrist. The pre-owned market, the truest read on end demand, has yet to confirm the rebound; resale values for the most-traded references remain well below their 2022 peak, and a genuine recovery would show up there before it showed up in a profit statement.

Underneath the group averages, the money is moving to the edges. Independent makers with waiting lists keep their pricing power while several group-owned brands fight discounting; the strongest markets are the ones, like the United States, where wealthy buyers are insulated from the macro weather. The June export jump is real and welcome, but it is a wholesale-channel event, and the channel has been wrong-footed before by reading its own restocking as demand.

The desk's view: an 11.2% export rebound is worth having, but a half-percent net margin is the number that tells you what kind of rebound it is. Volume returning to the wholesale pipe is not the same as customers returning to the counter, and until the pre-owned market turns and the profit line thickens, the desk treats June as a base effect flattered by restocking rather than proof the storm has passed. The exports came back first. The margin, and the resale tape, will say whether they meant it.
